title: Your First HTML Document
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of your first html document in a browser document.
Apply at least one relevant rule from this lesson to a small HTML example.
Check the result using browser inspection, a validator, or an accessibility checklist.

content.intro: A small, complete HTML document gives you a reliable starting point for every later topic: a doctype, root element, metadata, language, and body content.
content.why_it_matters: A clear foundation reduces syntax mistakes later and helps you read other people’s markup without treating it as mysterious code.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Writing your first HTML page is one of the decisions covered by Your First HTML Document. Decide what the markup is meant to communicate, choose the native HTML structure that expresses that meaning, and verify the result in a browser or a relevant validation checklist. Avoid using an element or attribute just because its default appearance seems convenient.

items.title: The <html> element
items.text: The root element encloses the document; the lang attribute belongs here in most complete documents.

items.title: The <head> element
items.text: The head contains document metadata and resource links rather than the ordinary visible page content.

items.title: The <body> element
items.text: The body contains the document content that the page presents to readers.

items.title: The <title> element
items.text: The title gives the document a concise name used by browser tabs, bookmarks, and search result contexts.

items.title: The lang attribute
items.text: The lang attribute: the natural language of the element’s text, which helps speech tools and text processing.

content_blocks.title: Keep in mind
content_blocks.text: Prefer the native semantic element that communicates intent. Do not choose markup solely for its default visual style.

content.task: Create a small HTML example that demonstrates your first html document. Keep the markup minimal, give every element a clear purpose, and inspect the rendered result.
task_acceptance_criteria: Use the relevant concept from Your First HTML Document.
Keep IDs unique and use valid nesting.
Check the result in a browser and record one finding.
hints: Start with the smallest valid example for your first html document.
Add one element or attribute at a time, then check the result.
Compare the source and rendered DOM if the behavior surprises you.
content.expected_output: The browser shows a page with the heading “Garden Notes” and a paragraph. The title appears in the browser tab.

troubleshooting.symptom: The expected content does not appear.
troubleshooting.check: Confirm the file was saved with an .html extension and inspect its path and nesting.
Check the resolved URL and confirm the referenced file or external resource exists and allows the request.

troubleshooting.symptom: The page looks correct but the markup may be invalid.
troubleshooting.check: Run the Nu Html Checker and follow its first relevant diagnostic, then validate again.

common_mistakes.why: The default appearance is not the element’s main meaning and can make navigation or maintenance harder.
common_mistakes.fix: Choose the element that matches the content purpose, then use CSS for presentation.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a browser’s recovery means the source is valid
common_mistakes.why: Browsers often recover from malformed markup, which can hide defects and produce unexpected document structure.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect the rendered DOM and run a validator against the original source.

common_mistakes.why: Missing files, narrow viewports, keyboard access, invalid input, or other states can expose defects.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected state plus one realistic edge case and an accessibility path.

summary: Your First HTML Document is about expressing document structure or behavior intentionally.

Understanding the minimum document structure is one of the decisions covered by Your First HTML Document. Decide what the markup is meant to communicate, choose the native HTML structure that expresses that meaning, and verify the result in a browser or a relevant validation checklist. Avoid using an element or attribute just because its default appearance seems convenient.
Verify both markup and behavior; do not infer correctness from appearance alone.
